title: Vertical vs. Horizontal Scaling Tradeoffs
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Software Architecture
description: Compare scaling up with scaling out for a workload: see the cost curve and hard ceiling of a bigger machine next to the Amdahl's Law throughput curve of more machines, and how many months each strategy lasts at a chosen growth rate.

educational.topic: Vertical and horizontal scaling, Amdahl's Law, and capacity planning
learningObjectives: Students will be able to compare vertical and horizontal scaling for a given workload by relating the cost curve and size ceiling of scaling up to the Amdahl's Law limit of scaling out, and estimate how long each strategy lasts at a given growth rate.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Side-by-side comparison with parameter exploration and a stated interpretation to test against
keyQuestions: What is the non-parallelizable fraction of this workload, and what limit does it set?
Which strategy runs out first at this growth rate, and what would extend it?
What does each strategy cost at the current load, and what does a single machine failure remove?
commonMisconceptions: Adding servers always adds proportional capacity (the serial fraction caps the speedup).
Vertical scaling is always the expensive option (at small sizes it costs about the same and needs no redesign).
A workload's parallelizable fraction is fixed (sharding, partitioning, and removing shared state raise it).
assessmentOpportunities: Give students a scenario (for example, "a stateful service at 5,000 requests per second growing 20% per month, with a measured serial fraction of 15%") and ask for the Amdahl limit, whether scaling out can carry the load in six months, and the ATAM finding they would record (risk, sensitivity point, or tradeoff point) with a justification.
